Navtlugi (Ashkenazi) Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Tbilisi, Georgia

Not demolished. Tbilisi's Jewish history stretches back over a millennium, with early references appearing in 12th- and 13th-century texts and a Jewish Karaite sect (the 'Tiflisites') founded there in the late 9th century. Ashkenazi Jewish migration from the Russian Empire began substantially in the 19th century - the city's Jewish population grew from just 105 in 1843 to 4,000 by 1903, and peaked around 20,000 by 1970 before declining to roughly 2,500 today. This cemetery, one of three historically serving Tbilisi's Jews, likely dates to the first half of the 19th century when Ashkenazi settlement began, though its oldest visible tombstone is dated 1892; it remains active, with burials as recent as 2020. Notable interments include Slava Shneerova (d. 1945), grandmother of former Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon. A memorial plaque credits philanthropist Abram Torner with funding the cemetery's administrative building and fence in 1897. Unlike many Tbilisi cemeteries destroyed under Soviet urban planning in the 1930s, Navtlughi reportedly survived 1960s clearance because its entrance was labeled 'Jewish-Russian,' leading Soviet authorities to spare it. The site is known as a 'Jewish Garden' for its distinctive Art Nouveau-influenced modernist gravestones from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
